case_study_insert.main_stem: PeakWest Renewables (PWR) is a private limited company in the renewable energy equipment sector, employing a workforce of 80. Founded in 2013 by Tomas Reid, it manufactures solar photovoltaic panels for commercial installers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. PWR plans to invest $960,000 in an automated solar-cell assembly line with offcut recycling, financed by a $560,000 ten-year bank loan and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $30 a unit and a selling price of $45, and currently produces 48,000 units a year. PWR faces a quality problem: the panel defect rate has reached 3.4% and labour turnover is rising, while its plant reports growing material waste from older cutting machines.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Report — Q3 2025: The plant produced 12,000 panels last quarter at a defect rate of 3.4%, up from 1.7% a year ago. Customer complaints rose from 19 to 37 per month. Average order lead time is 4.6 days. Material waste is 6.2% of inputs and energy use is 2.1 kWh per panel. A skills audit shows 22 of 80 production staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new assembly machines; off-the-job training at the technical college is also being considered. A staff survey found 22 of 80 workers felt their views were ignored under the current autocratic leadership, with democratic leadership and laissez-faire leadership suggested as alternatives. HR is also considering a bonus scheme linked to quality.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of PeakWest Renewables for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $12.60 to $13.60 an hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across manufacturing. (3) Polysilicon and silver input costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year, renewable-equipment inflation is 8.4%, and demand for commercial solar installations grew 6.0%.

questions.question_text: PWR plans to fund part of its $960,000 assembly line with $400,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for PWR of using retained profit instead of the $560,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment schedule, so it protects PWR's cash flow while the firm already bears fixed costs of $300,000 a year and is taking on a $560,000 bank loan. The money saved can be spent on reducing the 3.4% defect rate and the 6.2% material waste without raising the $45 selling price to commercial installers. With the base rate rising to 5.25% (Appendix 3), debt will get dearer, so funding part of the line internally reduces exposure to that increase.

Point 2: Using $400,000 retained profit preserves the ownership and control of founder Tomas Reid and the existing shareholders, with no lender conditions attached to the $960,000 investment. There is also no collateral risk: if the new assembly line fails to cut the 3.4% defect rate, the automated machines cannot be repossessed. Retained profit can be released immediately, allowing the offcut-recycling equipment to be installed before the next order cycle rather than waiting for loan approval.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to PWR and the case data.

questions.question_text: PWR is launching a high-efficiency solar panel for commercial installers. Consider national television advertising, trade magazine advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should PWR choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: TV would create rapid, mass awareness of the high-efficiency panel and could support premium pricing at the $45 selling price. However, airtime is very expensive for an 80-employee manufacturer funding a $960,000 line, and most viewers are households rather than the commercial installers who actually buy the panels, so much of the budget would be wasted.

Trade magazine advertising: Specialist solar and construction titles reach exactly the commercial installers PWR supplies, allowing detailed technical claims about efficiency and the 3.4% defect-rate improvement programme to be made credibly. Costs are far lower than television. The limits are a narrow readership and long lead times, so trade press alone may not build enough demand to use the 48,000-unit capacity quickly.

Social media influencer marketing: Instagram and video influencers in the renewable sector can demonstrate panels visually and generate engagement, especially as demand for commercial solar installations grew 6.0%. The audience is mixed consumers and trade, and results depend on influencer credibility, but cost per reached buyer is low.

Recommendation: PWR should choose trade magazine advertising. It targets the commercial installers who actually place the 12,000-panel quarterly orders and can carry the technical message needed after a 3.4% defect rate, at a fraction of television's cost. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted; influencers are rejected as too consumer-focused for a business-to-business panel maker. PWR can add limited social media content later.

Trade press also lets PWR publish the 2.1 kWh energy-use figure and the offcut-recycling story, differentiating its panels from rivals and supporting the $45 price with credible technical detail aimed at the installers who place the 12,000 quarterly orders.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with minimal reference to PWR's commercial installers.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options with PWR context and some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of PWR's buyers, defect rate and capacity, with a justified recommendation explaining why television and influencers are rejected.

questions.question_text: PWR's 3.4% defect rate and rising labour turnover are damaging quality. Explain two benefits for PWR of introducing a bonus scheme linked to defect rates.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A quality-linked bonus gives the 80 production staff a direct financial incentive to reduce the 3.4% defect rate, which is up from 1.7% a year ago. Because pay is tied to measured quality, workers have a reason to check panels carefully and report faults early, cutting the 6.2% material waste and the 37 monthly complaints and protecting the $45 price PWR charges commercial installers.

Point 2: A bonus can improve motivation and retention where autocratic leadership has left 22 of 80 workers feeling their views are ignored. Sharing in the gains from fewer defects makes staff feel rewarded and valued, which can reduce the rising labour turnover and the cost of repeatedly training replacements on the new assembly machines. It also supports the $960,000 investment, since a lower defect rate means more of the 48,000-unit output is sellable rather than scrapped.

Because the bonus is paid only when measured defects fall, it also gives PWR an objective way to test whether the $960,000 automated line is working, linking pay to the 1.7% defect benchmark of a year ago rather than to output volume alone.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to PWR and the case data.

questions.question_text: PWR must train 22 staff on the new assembly machines. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the technical college. Which should PWR choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the assembly line is specific to PWR's own machines and quality standards and costs no course fees, while the 22 staff keep producing from the 48,000-unit target. It can be delivered immediately to tackle the 3.4% defect rate. However, the trainers are production workers whose output suffers, bad habits may be passed on, and there is no formal certificate, which may matter when commercial installers audit quality.

Off-the-job training: The technical college course gives structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised qualification for all 22 staff, which helps address the 1.7%-to-3.4% defect deterioration and the 37 monthly complaints. It costs fees and removes 22 of 80 staff from the line, reducing short-term capacity, and the generic content may not match PWR's exact settings, so some on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: PWR should choose off-the-job training for the 22 staff, followed by short on-site coaching. Formal technical certification is worth the disruption because the defect rate has doubled to 3.4% and complaints have risen to 37; on-the-job training alone is rejected because it would pass on current bad habits and offers no proof of competence to the commercial installers who buy the 12,000 panels produced each quarter.

A phased programme would let one group attend the technical college while the rest keep the 12,000-panel quarterly output flowing, limiting disruption. It also gives PWR time to measure whether the defect rate falls towards the 1.7% benchmark before committing the remaining staff, protecting the $400,000 retained profit and the 3.4%-quality target.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with little application to PWR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of both methods in PWR's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensively evaluates both methods against cost, disruption and quality needs, with a clear decision and explicit reasons for rejecting the alternative.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how PWR's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $300,000 ÷ ($45 − $30) = $300,000 ÷ $15 = 20,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 20,000 panels a year.

sub_parts.question_text: Calculate PWR's average total cost per unit.
sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Average total cost = Fixed costs ÷ Output + Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $300,000 ÷ 48,000 = $6.25; $6.25 + $30 = $36.25. Answer: average total cost is $36.25 a panel.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways PWR's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Break-even of 20,000 units against output of 48,000 gives a margin of safety of 28,000 panels, showing how far sales could fall before a loss.
2. With average total cost of $36.25 and a $45 price, managers can see a $8.75 potential margin per panel and judge whether the 11.3% polysilicon and silver rise can be absorbed.
3. The $15 contribution helps test whether the $560,000 bank loan can be serviced before the $960,000 line is extended further.
4. Tracking unit cost each quarter highlights the 6.2% material waste and the impact of the 3.4% defect rate, guiding the offcut-recycling investment.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 20,000 units | (ii) Average total cost = $36.25 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 28,000 panels; price-versus-cost margin of $8.75 under 11.3% input inflation; loan servicing on the $560,000 debt; and unit-cost control of 6.2% waste and the 3.4% defect rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate PWR's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has PWR's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 30.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 35.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 16.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit $960,000 ÷ revenue $3,200,000 × 100 = 30.0; 2025 $1,260,000 ÷ $3,600,000 × 100 = 35.0. Operating profit $384,000 ÷ revenue $3,200,000 × 100 = 12.0 in 2024 and $540,000 ÷ $3,600,000 × 100 = 15.0 in 2025. Returns on capital: $384,000 ÷ $2,400,000 × 100 = 16.0 in 2024 and $540,000 ÷ $2,700,000 × 100 = 20.0 in 2025. Cost of sales rose only from $2,240,000 to $2,340,000 while revenue rose $400,000, so gross profit grew by $300,000. Interest payable fell from $40,000 to $35,000.

Evaluation: All three measures improved. The gross margin rose from 30.0% to 35.0%, indicating better control of panel production costs even as polysilicon and silver prices climbed 11.3%. The operating margin improved from 12.0% to 15.0%, so more profit survives the $300,000 fixed costs. Returns on capital increased from 16.0% to 20.0%, showing the $2,700,000 of capital employed is working harder. The improvement is supported by real growth in revenue and gross profit, not just cost cutting. The risk is that a 3.4% defect rate and 6.2% material waste could undo these gains if the $960,000 assembly line is not managed well, and higher interest costs may reduce the benefit.

Conclusion: PWR's financial performance has improved. The gross margin (30.0% to 35.0%), operating margin (12.0% to 15.0%) and returns on capital (16.0% to 20.0%) all rose together, backed by higher revenue and gross profit. PWR should protect this by using part of the $400,000 retained profit to cut the 3.4% defect rate before expanding further.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or simple changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates all three ratios for both years with some contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital and interest, and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for PWR of introducing offcut recycling on its solar panel assembly line.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recycling offcuts directly reduces the 6.2% of material currently wasted and cushions the 11.3% rise in polysilicon and silver input costs reported in Appendix 3. Lower material waste cuts the $30 variable cost per panel, protecting the $15 contribution and making the $960,000 assembly line more attractive; it also supports PWR's renewable-energy brand with commercial installers.

Disadvantage: The recycling equipment forms part of the $960,000 outlay and must be funded alongside a $560,000 bank loan while the base rate rises to 5.25%, so cash flow could be tight if demand grows more slowly than the 6.0% forecast. Recycling also needs staff trained on new sorting routines, which is hard while labour turnover is rising and 22 of 80 workers lack training; until the 3.4% defect rate is fixed, recycled material could even quality risk if not carefully controlled.

Recycling also reduces dependence on the 11.3%-dearer polysilicon and silver inputs and supports the renewable-energy positioning of the business with the commercial installers who buy the 12,000 panels made each quarter.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to PWR and the case data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.25%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in polysilicon and silver input costs will affect PWR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate (4.5% to 5.25%): If PWR's $560,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $560,000 = $4,200 a year (0.0075 × $560,000). That is small relative to fixed costs of $300,000 a year and would be zero on a fixed-rate loan. Higher rates could also make commercial installers delay projects and raise the cost of future borrowing for the $960,000 line, but the direct effect is bounded.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $13.60 an hour): With a workforce of 80 in production roles, this raises the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total cannot be invented; the proper test is productivity, 48,000 panels ÷ 80 staff = 600 panels per worker. If output per worker holds and the 3.4% defect rate falls, the rise is affordable; otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $15 contribution narrows.

Input-cost inflation (11.3% polysilicon and silver): The $30 variable cost is not broken down in the insert, so only a bound is honest: if the whole $30 rose 11.3%, that adds 11.3% × $30 = $3.39 a panel; across 48,000 panels a year that is about $162,720 (48,000 × $3.39). That would cut contribution from $15.00 towards $11.61 on every panel, far exceeding the interest effect, and it comes on top of 6.2% material waste. Only part can be recovered through price negotiations with installers.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in polysilicon and silver input costs will have the greatest impact. It hits all 48,000 panels and directly erodes the $15 contribution that underpins the $960,000 investment, whereas the interest rise is a bounded $4,200 a year and the wage rise can be absorbed if productivity holds at 600 panels per worker. PWR should cut the 6.2% waste first.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to PWR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on PWR's costs, revenue or financing in context, using insert figures.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes in PWR's context with a well-justified judgement that input cost inflation has the greatest impact and clear reasons why the other two are smaller.
